issues: The correction says 'MPs in 1960 defended it as protection against peeping Toms and eavesdroppers'. In fact the phrase was one MP's, Peter Rawlinson (Epsom). He used it for the repeal bill, not the Act: 'a modest charter for peeping Toms and eavesdroppers'. The House then refused leave, Ayes 148, Noes 230 (HC Deb 26 January 1960 vol 616 cc50-60). The wording is made precise below.

The correction's claim that the binding-over power 'was later used against eavesdroppers' had no source. Blackstone (Book IV, 'Of the means of preventing offences') ties the power to 34 Edw. III c. 1 and lists 'eaves-droppers' among those a justice may bind over under its 'not of good fame' words. Added.

Checked OK: the revised text on legislation.gov.uk names offenders, rioters and barrators and sureties from those [not] of good Fame, and never mentions eavesdroppers or peeping toms. Note that 'not' is bracketed as an editorial insertion (X4), and in the 1960 debate Leslie Hale said the word is missing from the Parliament roll. That does not affect the myth verdict.

The GILC page is the 1998 Privacy and Human Rights survey. Its acknowledgements say it was written by Privacy International, with primary authors David Banisar (EPIC) and Simon Davies (PI). '1998' is the most frequent year cited on the page (943 times), so the approximate date holds.

fieldFixes.correction: The 1361 statute names neither peeping toms nor eavesdroppers. It lets justices restrain offenders, rioters and barrators, and take sureties of good behaviour from people 'not of good fame'. Later lawyers read those general words broadly: Blackstone's Commentaries (Book IV, 1769) says a justice may bind over 'eaves-droppers' under them. In 1960, opposing a bill to repeal the Act, the MP Peter Rawlinson called the repeal bill 'a modest charter for peeping Toms and eavesdroppers', and the Commons refused leave by 230 votes to 148. The privacy reading comes from later practice, not from the text.

issues: No errors found. Semayne's Case was decided in the King's Bench in Michaelmas Term 1604 (5 Co Rep 91a). Coke was then Attorney General (1594–1606) and reported it; he was not a judge until 1606. Coke's Latin 'domus sua cuique est tutissimum refugium' is on the OLL page, and Digest 2.4.18 (Gaius, 1 ad l. xii tab.) reads 'quia domus tutissimum cuique refugium atque receptaculum sit'.

The Lambarde claim rested only on a party-aligned amicus brief. I found a primary check: the 1591 Eirenarcha (Internet Archive scan of the 1591 edition, Book 2, ch. 5 on Riots, p. 188) says a man may gather company to defend himself because 'his house, is his Hold and Castle'. That confirms Lambarde used the castle maxim before 1604. The exact sentence the brief quotes from p. 257 ('our law calleth a man's house, his castle ...') could not be found in the garbled OCR, so it stays attributed to the brief. Both Lambarde and Coke's report cite the Year Book 21 Hen. 7. 39, which shows the idea's older roots.

issues: The correction is wrong to call the maxim 'a paraphrase' and the words 'descriptive, not a command'. Royer-Collard used the exact words himself in the 1827 Chamber debate on the press bill (the 'loi de justice et d'amour'). Speaking against article 20, which let prosecutors pursue any publication about private life, he said: 'Je répéterai volontiers ce que j'ai dit en 1819 ...; oui, la vie privée doit être murée ... La vie privée doit être murée, mais contre quoi? contre ce qui lui est ennemi apparemment, c'est-à-dire contre la diffamation'. Source: Barante, La vie politique de M. Royer-Collard, vol. 2. So the maxim is his own, from 1827, presented as a restatement of 1819. The myth's real error is the date and wording given to the 1819 speech. The verdict stays MISLEADING; the correction is rewritten.

The claim that the 1819 law does not use 'vie privée' had no quote attached. Halpérin says it directly: 'L'expression « vie privée » n'apparaît pas dans la loi' (the press law of 17 May 1819). Added. The correction now names that law.

Checked OK: Halpérin gives the 1819 speech's date as 27 April 1819 and the wording 'voilà donc la vie privée murée ... elle est déclarée invisible, elle est renfermée dans l'intérieur des maisons'. I could not reach an independent 1819 text (Archives parlementaires, 2e série, for 1819 is not on the Internet Archive), so the date rests on Halpérin.

fieldFixes.correction: The words are Royer-Collard's own, but not from 1819. In his speech of 27 April 1819 on the press laws he said, descriptively, 'voilà donc la vie privée murée ... elle est déclarée invisible, elle est renfermée dans l'intérieur des maisons' — so there is private life walled in. The maxim 'la vie privée doit être murée' comes from his speech in the 1827 Chamber debate on a new press bill, where he said he was repeating what he had said in 1819. He then limited it at once: private life should be walled in against defamation, not against the publication of indifferent or honourable acts. The press law of 17 May 1819 itself does not use the expression 'vie privée'.
